sentences.text: The skull of this giant measured 70 centimetres in length, a size paleontologists view as relatively small for such a massive animal.
Its leg bones were substantial, with the femur reaching approximately 2.2 meters in length.
This creature holds the title of the largest dinosaur ever discovered in Europe and ranks among the biggest known worldwide.
One scientist suggested the head was small because a larger one might have caused the animal to break its neck.
Remains were first found on May 23, 2003, at El Húmero, located just one kilometer from the town of Riodeva in the province of Teruel, Spain.
The species, named after the locality where the fossils were found, was officially described by Royo-Torres, Cobos, and Alcalá in 2006.
Its genus name combines the Turia River in Teruel with the Greek word for lizard.
Early calculations based on a 1.79-meter humerus and other bones suggested the animal reached 36 to 38 meters in length and weighed between 39.9 and 47.36 tonnes.
More recent estimates suggest Turiasaurus was 21 to 30 meters long and weighed between 30 and 50 tonnes.
Phylogenetic analysis places Turiasaurus outside the Neosauropoda division within a new clade called Turiasauria, alongside Losillasaurus and Galvesaurus.
This giant is the first of its kind identified in the Turiasauria clade, whereas other large sauropods like Diplodocus, Brachiosaurus, and Argentinosaurus belong to the Neosauropoda clade.
Turiasaurus riodevensis lived during the Kimmeridgian stage of the Late Jurassic and is known from fossils found in the Villar del Arzobispo Formation of Teruel, Spain.
The animal lived during the Late Jurassic, approximately 155 to 146 million years ago, spanning from the Kimmeridgian to the Tithonian stages in what is now Europe.
Approximately 150 million years ago, the habitat was an extensive tidal plain cut by large rivers flowing into the Tethys Sea.
